extracted.intended_audience: scholarly publishers, journal editors, research policy‑makers, meta‑researchers, and others interested in peer review innovation
extracted.subtask_description: Frameworks and criteria for evaluating and designing peer review systems and innovations (e.g., open review, portable review, registered reports), including trade‑offs between quality, transparency, equity, and efficiency. Aimed at informing policy, editorial decisions, and experimentation in scholarly publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality & Reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on improving the way journals decide which manuscripts to accept or reject and on ensuring the robustness and reproducibility of published research (e.g., registered reports; peer review of data and software).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promotes rigorous methods and in‑depth checks (registered reports decide acceptance on research plans rather than results). May require more reviewers per manuscript or extended scope (data/software), increasing reviewer workload. May favour knowledge of author identity to evaluate context or conflicts. Could narrow the notion of 'quality' and unintentionally disadvantage research types or groups not aligned with that notion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy & Transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasis on openness in peer review: publishing reviewer identities and review reports, 'publish, then review' models, and reducing the primacy of binary accept/reject decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aims to increase accountability, enable broader participation, and reduce gatekeeping. Examples include open peer review and post‑publication review. Risks include reduced candour from reviewers (especially early career reviewers facing power asymmetries) and incompatibility with double‑anonymous workflows and preprinting (which reveals authorship).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity & Inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Make peer review more equitable and inclusive by increasing diversity in reviewer pools and editorial boards and adopting practices to reduce bias (e.g., double‑anonymous review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addresses underrepresentation and differential outcomes across gender and other groups. Diversity targets and double‑anonymity are suggested measures, but imposing targets may make finding reviewers harder and may disrupt existing informal reward systems. Also recognizes that notions of 'quality' can favour certain research types and thereby disadvantage some social groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiency & Incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce reviewer burden and make peer review more efficient, while providing incentives and recognition for reviewers (e.g., portable peer review, Publons/ORCID recognition, paying reviewers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initiatives: portable/cascading review within or across publishers, MECA submission interoperability, Review Commons (journal‑independent review), and platforms that record/recognize review work. Trade‑offs: efficiency measures may clash with quality (journals may prefer trusted reviewers) and some incentive approaches (e.g., publishing reviewer identities) may deter reviewers. Paying reviewers is proposed but may be financially unsustainable (e.g., suggested $450/review).

rubrics_metrics.name: Portable Peer Review / Reuse of Review Reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Enable reuse of review reports when manuscripts move between journals, via cascading within publisher portfolios or cross‑publisher initiatives (e.g., Neuroscience Peer Review Consortium).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduces re‑review work and publication delays by transferring reviews to subsequent journals. Technical and cultural challenges remain. Journals concerned about quality may prefer their own known reviewers rather than relying on external reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal‑Independent Peer Review (Review Commons model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts are posted as preprints and undergo peer review independent of a target journal; authors can then submit revised manuscripts plus reports to participating journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: assesses study quality rather than journal fit, accelerates communication, and allows transfer of referee reports to avoid repeated cycles. Relies on preprinting and participating journal networks; intended to reduce reviewer time spent on repeated assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open Peer Review Practice (publish reports and/or reviewer identities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing reviewer reports and sometimes reviewer identities to increase transparency, accountability, and credit for reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Has been implemented variably (e.g., BMC publishes reports, formerly identities). Benefits: exposes judgments, may reduce bias, gives recognition. Downsides: may reduce willingness to provide critical reviews (Van Rooyen et al. found negative effect on willingness), especially among vulnerable reviewers. Policy design should consider optional vs mandatory identity publication and potential chilling effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity vs Transparency Balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing appropriate levels/timing of anonymity: single‑anonymous, double‑anonymous, open review, or hybrid approaches (e.g., double‑blind pre‑publication and transparent post‑publication review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each approach has trade‑offs: double‑anonymous can reduce bias but is incompatible with preprinting and difficult in small communities; open review increases accountability but may reduce frankness; hybrid models (IOP Publishing) attempt to combine objectivity during review with transparency after publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition and Validation of Reviewing Work
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide visibility and formal recognition for peer review activities (platforms like Publons, ORCID integration, publishing reviews where allowed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended to incentivize reviewing by making invisible labour visible and citable. Implementations vary; recognition may increase participation but depends on perceived value and how it maps onto academic rewards. Validation and trustworthy tracking are important (calls to build incentives and trust through validation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment for Peer Review
rubrics_metrics.description: Directly compensate reviewers financially for their work (proposed amounts discussed in debate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proponents argue it could speed up review and improve quality. Critics point to sustainability concerns (e.g., $450 per review suggested) and insufficient funds in current system. Payment may change intrinsic motivations and the gift economy dynamic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registered Reports
rubrics_metrics.description: A publication model where acceptance/rejection decisions are made on the basis of a detailed research plan before results are known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aims to reduce publication bias and improve research quality and reproducibility. Evidence (e.g., Soderberg et al., Chambers & Tzavella) suggests registered reports can improve research quality versus standard models. Implementation requires editorial commitment and may shift review emphasis to study design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post‑Publication Peer Review and Community Feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Use open, community‑based feedback after publication (or after preprinting) as a complement or alternative to traditional pre‑publication gatekeeping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can reduce reliance on binary acceptance, be relatively inexpensive, and increase democratic participation. Works well as a complement to a basic quality assurance process; requires platforms and incentives for community engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heterogeneous System with Basic QA + Selective In‑Depth Review
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed model where every work gets a basic quality check, and select works (high interest/importance) receive additional, rigorous peer review focused on reproducibility and robustness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combines efficiency (basic, low‑cost assurance) with capacity for high‑quality scrutiny where warranted. Should be implemented equitably and account for disciplinary variation. Helps reconcile competing aims of different schools of thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence‑Informed Policy and Experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Design and adopt peer review innovations based on rigorous empirical study of peer review, with stakeholders intensifying efforts to study and experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calls for coordinated, evidence‑based action by publishers, funders, institutions, societies, and researchers. References to research calls (Rennie; Squazzoni et al.) emphasize making peer review itself a subject of investigation to guide policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of Academic Recognition and Reward Structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for how peer review models interact with academic evaluation systems (prestige, impact factors) and reforms in research assessment (responsible assessment, EDI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journal prestige and impact metrics shape stakeholders' willingness to experiment. Moving away from crude metrics and adopting responsible assessment practices may increase openness to new peer review models. Policy should align review innovations with broader assessment reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing Trade‑offs Between Diversity Targets and Reviewer Availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate implications of imposing diversity targets for reviewer pools and editorial boards on practical ability to recruit reviewers and on existing reward economies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While diversity is desirable long‑term, targets may in the short term make reviewer recruitment harder and upset gift‑economy recognition pathways. Long‑term sustainability gains from diversity should be weighed against short‑term operational challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability Mechanisms to Reduce Bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Use transparency and other accountability practices (e.g., publishing reports) to expose or reduce reviewer biases and improve fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open review may expose biases and increase accountability; empirical studies (e.g., Bruce et al., studies of bias) inform potential effectiveness. However, publication of identities can also reduce reviewers' willingness to critique and may not eliminate subtle forms of bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer Pool and Scope Management (workload implications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions about number of reviewers per manuscript and expansion of review scope (e.g., to datasets and code) which affect workload and system sustainability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increasing reviewers or expanding scope supports quality & reproducibility but increases burden, raising concerns from efficiency perspectives. Solutions require incentives, recognition, or technological/process innovations to manage load.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for Disciplinary Variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy and innovation should leave room for differences across disciplines; not all peer review approaches are equally suitable everywhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognizes that some innovations are more relevant in particular fields (e.g., registered reports in some domains). Flexible systems that allow disciplinary variation are recommended to avoid one‑size‑fits‑all mismatches.
